notes.meaning: Jeremiah now gives God's message against Babylon, the great empire of that day. The king of Babylon had been kind to Jeremiah, yet he still had to speak its doom. Friendship with people does not let a prophet hide God's warning. Jeremiah stresses that the words come from God, not from himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have argued that Jeremiah did not write this long prophecy and that a later writer added it. Others answer that its words, pictures, and style match the rest of Jeremiah.

notes.meaning: God tells His people to spread the news everywhere and hold nothing back: Babylon has fallen. The fall is so certain that it is spoken of as already done. Bel and Marduk were Babylon's chief gods, and they are put to shame because they could not save their own city. The idols were only carved wood and stone.

An enemy from the north will come. This means the Medes and Persians, who lived north of Babylon. The land will become empty of people and animals. Later attacks finished what this first defeat began, until Babylon became a lonely ruin.

When Babylon falls, the people of Israel and Judah will come back together. They weep as they come, out of sorrow for their sins and joy at God's mercy. They turn back to God first, and then to their land. They ask the way to Zion, God's holy city, and bind themselves to Him in a covenant (a lasting promise between God and His people) that will never be forgotten. Many see here a picture of anyone who turns to God in true repentance.

God calls His people lost sheep. Their leaders, both kings and priests, led them astray into idol worship on the hills. They wandered from one false god to another. They forgot their true resting place, which was God Himself.

Enemies treated Israel like stray sheep anyone could eat. They excused their cruelty by saying, "They sinned against their God, so we are not to blame." Israel's sin was real, but it did not make their enemies innocent. Without knowing it, the enemies also spoke the truth that God was still Israel's true home and hope.

God tells His people to leave Babylon as soon as the door opens. They should be like the male goats that walk boldly at the front of the flock. Each should want to be first and set a good example for others.

God Himself stirs up a great alliance of nations from the north to attack Babylon. Their archers are so skilled and strong that their arrows never miss. Babylon has robbed others, and now it will be robbed until its attackers have all they want.

Babylon gloated as it plundered God's people, His "inheritance". It was like a well-fed young cow kicking up its heels, or like proud horses neighing. So Babylon, the "mother" of its people, will be put to shame. Once the queen of the world, it will become the least of nations, a dry desert.
Babylon will become empty because of God's anger. People passing by will be shocked. They will hiss in scorn instead of feeling pity.

God calls the archers to surround Babylon and shoot without holding back. The reason is that Babylon sinned against the Lord. God used Babylon to correct His people, but Babylon acted out of cruelty and greed. God treats harm done to His people as harm done to Himself.

The attackers shout as they close in, and Babylon gives up. Its walls and towers fall. This is God's just payback: as Babylon did to others, so it will suffer. This was God's own judgment. It does not give anyone permission to take personal revenge.
No one will be left to plant or harvest the fields. Foreigners who lived or fought for Babylon will flee home in fear. The land will be emptied of people.

Israel is like a lone sheep chased by lions. First Assyria devoured the northern tribes. Then Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon crushed what was left, like a lion breaking the bones. God speaks with tender pity for His hurting people.
So God will punish Babylon's king just as He punished Assyria. Assyria's fall was a known example. It assured God's people that Babylon would fall too.

God will bring His sheep home to rich pasture. Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim, and Gilead were the most fruitful parts of the land. Like a faithful shepherd, God will feed and protect them until they are fully satisfied.

This is the root of all the blessings: God will forgive. People will search for Israel's and Judah's sins and find none, because God has wiped them away. This mercy is for the "remnant", the small group God keeps for Himself, and it comes only by His grace. It points ahead to the new covenant and the full forgiveness given through Christ.

God orders the attackers against Babylon. "Merathaim" sounds like "double rebellion" and "Pekod" like "punishment". The names show that Babylon was very rebellious and that its time of punishment had come. Some take them as real places on the way to Babylon. "Devote to destruction" means to destroy completely. Cyrus and his armies did not know God, yet they carried out what God had planned.

The sounds of war and great ruin fill the land. Babylon had been like a hammer that smashed nations all over the earth. Now the hammer itself is broken, and people are amazed at how far it has fallen. Some apply the hammer picture to Nebuchadnezzar himself, the one who crushed so many peoples.
